name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
worldviewSummary: Rousseau argues that social development, property and dependence corrupted natural human goodness and produced inequality and amour-propre (a competitive self-love dependent on others' opinion). Legitimate political order requires a social contract in which citizens obey only the general will they themselves make, achieving moral freedom.
biography: Genevan-born writer and philosopher active in France. His Discourse on the Arts and Sciences (1750) won the Dijon Academy prize; the Social Contract and Emile (both 1762) were condemned and burned in Paris and Geneva.

works.title: Discourse on the Origin and Foundations of Inequality among Men
Discourse on the Arts and Sciences

concepts.description: The will of the body politic directed at the common good, distinct from the sum of private wills; laws are legitimate when they express it.
A relative, socially generated self-love that depends on comparison with and esteem from others, a source of vanity and inequality.
Obedience to a law one prescribes to oneself is freedom, whereas the impulse of appetite alone is slavery.

positions.statement: Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains; the task is to find a form of association under which each, uniting with all, still obeys only himself.
The progress of the arts and sciences has not purified morals but has accompanied luxury, idleness and the corruption of civic virtue.
The first person who enclosed land and said 'this is mine', and found people simple enough to believe it, was the founder of civil society — and of the crimes, wars and miseries inequality brought.
Education should follow the child's natural development, learning first from things and experience rather than from books and authority.
Sovereignty cannot be represented; a people that gives itself representatives is no longer free in the full sense.

relations.note: Criticizes property-centred accounts of civil society (scholarly comparison).
